Report an unassociated account as \\\\\"not accessible from this\\\\nAgent Space\\\\\".\\\\n\\\\n## Step 2: Pass 1 \\\\u2014 Discover\\\\n\\\\nCloudFront is a global service. **Make every CloudFront, ACM-for-CloudFront, and CloudWatch\\\\ncall in `us-east-1`, and do not iterate regions.**\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\ncloudfront.ListDistributions                  # paginate on Marker / NextMarker until null (\\\\u2264100 per page)\\\\ncloudfront.GetDistributionConfig              # per distribution: Logging and ContinuousDeploymentPolicyId are not in the summary\\\\ncloudfront.ListOriginAccessControls\\\\ncloudfront.ListCloudFrontOriginAccessIdentities\\\\ncloudfront.ListCachePolicies                  # Type=custom, plus managed policies referenced by behaviors\\\\ncloudfront.ListOriginRequestPolicies\\\\ncloudfront.ListResponseHeadersPolicies\\\\ncloudfront.ListRealtimeLogConfigs\\\\ncloudfront.ListContinuousDeploymentPolicies\\\\ncloudfront.ListKeyGroups\\\\ncloudfront.ListFunctions                      # metadata only\\\\ncloudfront.GetMonitoringSubscription          # per distribution: are additional metrics on?\\\\nlogs.DescribeDeliverySources                  # us-east-1: standard logging (v2) sources for distributions\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`ListDistributions` returns, per distribution, its origins, cache behaviors, viewer\\\\ncertificate, `WebACLId`, restrictions, HTTP version, price class and custom error\\\\nresponses. **It does not return `Logging`.** A logging verdict is only valid after\\\\n`GetDistributionConfig` has run for that distribution. Looking at EEXAMPLE000038, I realize the SEC-04 SSLv3 check applies to any CustomOriginConfig regardless of whether it's a website endpoint, since there's no website exception carved out for that rule specifically - only SEC-02 has that exception. So even though one origin is an s3-website type with the website exception for SEC-02, it still gets hit with SEC-04 CRITICAL because its SSL protocols list includes SSLv3. Combined with another origin that properly uses OAC and the allow-all SEC-01 CRITICAL, this distribution stacks two criticals too. Next I'm checking EEXAMPLE000090, which has four origins, several correctly configured with OAC.

For EEXAMPLE000090, I see it also has an allow-all CRITICAL, but its cache behavior properly uses TrustedKeyGroups for signed URLs on a jpeg path, which is good practice, so overall it's lower severity than previous ones. Moving to the ServerlessImageHandler stacks EEXAMPLE000030 and EEXAMPLE000105, the API Gateway origin's SSL protocols include TLSv1.1 which triggers SEC-04 HIGH, though the default behavior redirects to HTTPS and custom error responses are properly configured, so this one only stacks a single HIGH issue - moderate severity overall. Then I start looking at a cluster of stacks (EEXAMPLE000066, EEXAMPLE000098, EEXAMPLE000052, EEXAMPLE000049) that all use OAC correctly, but their ACM certificates use the older MinimumProtocolVersion TLSv1_2016, which fails SEC-05 as HIGH.

Within that cluster, EEXAMPLE000098 also has the allow-all CRITICAL stacked with the SEC-05 HIGH, while EEXAMPLE000066 redirects to HTTPS properly but still carries the TLSv1_2016 SEC-05 HIGH. EEXAMPLE000092 also fails SEC-05 HIGH with a newer but still inadequate TLS policy, combined with being disabled and using SNI-only SSL support, and EEXAMPLE000080 similarly fails SEC-05 HIGH with TLSv1_2016 while also being disabled. EEXAMPLE000109 doesn't add much beyond the allow-all CRITICAL and two medium-severity legacy OAI findings.

Given the time I've spent, I'm ready to finalize the worst-10 ranking by prioritizing CRITICAL count first, then HIGH count, then overall number of findings. My top candidate is EEXAMPLE000091 with three criticals (one SEC-01 plus two SEC-02 origin instances) plus a HIGH for missing WAF on a dynamic behavior and two medium severity findings. EEXAMPLE000010 follows with two criticals - the allow-all SEC-01 and an SSLv3 SEC-04 issue, plus a default cert that needs inspection under SEC-05. I'm now starting to evaluate EEXAMPLE000039's SEC-01 finding to see where it ranks.

That self-referencing CDP field on EEXAMPLE000098 looks like a stale artifact — no other distribution shares that pointer, so I'll treat it as orphaned with no real primary, flagging it as an INFO item rather than pairing it.

Now I'm ranking the top findings by severity and impact, starting with EEXAMPLE000091 which stacks multiple criticals plus a high for missing WAF, then moving into the next candidate.

For the rest of the top ten I'm cataloging distributions with paired CRITICAL findings — allow-all policies combined with SSLv3 origins, weak TLS, or missing OAC — noting specifics like the staging distribution carrying 10% live production traffic through a weak config, and flagging SSLv3 as severe enough to include even when the rest of the distribution is otherwise hardened. I land on EEXAMPLE000098 itself as a strong candidate too, given its allow-all CRITICAL paired with a weak viewer security policy despite having OAC properly configured.

I'm now weighing a couple of borderline HIGH-severity candidates, like the API Gateway Image Handler backend's weak TLS version and a stack with an unexpectedly solid ACM cert that still fails the baseline allow-all check — a good illustration that TLS hardening doesn't excuse the separate security-group misconfiguration. Before finalizing the list I want to double-check a few more distributions from the batches I haven't fully reviewed yet, in case there's an additional origin issue I'm missing.

Re-examining batch 1's origin configs more carefully, I catch one I'd overlooked: a custom origin pointed at httpbin.org with an http-only origin protocol policy, which is a critical misconfiguration since it's not a website-exception case but a real custom origin — and since the default cache behavior targets that same origin, an allow-all viewer policy would compound the problem by routing insecure traffic straight through.

So this distribution likely has two criticals — the allow-all viewer policy and the http-only custom origin — plus a medium issue from a missing cache policy combined with forwarded values. The distribution being disabled lowers real-world exposure but doesn't change the severity rating of the config itself.

Moving to the next one, a single S3 origin with OAI and no custom origin config, I'm only flagging the allow-all viewer policy as critical, and this one's also disabled.

Then there's EEXAMPLE000044, whose origin uses an https-only policy (fine) but still allows TLSv1 and TLSv1.1, which is a high-severity finding alongside the allow-all critical — another stacked critical+high case. EEXAMPLE000035 is already covered under the http-only media issue. EEXAMPLE000075 is a single S3 OAI case with just the allow-all critical, but I want to flag it separately since it's the one distribution with additional metrics enabled, worth revisiting in a second pass.

Several more distributions follow the same single S3 OAI pattern with only the allow-all critical: EEXAMPLE000093 and EEXAMPLE000070 (af-south-1). EEXAMPLE000021 uses an S3 website endpoint origin with an http-only policy, which is a medium exception, plus the allow-all critical. EEXAMPLE000024 is more serious — its origin is a custom ALB with an http-only policy, which triggers a critical SEC-02 finding on top of the allow-all critical, giving it two criticals, and it also has weak TLS versions enabled.

I'm treating that TLS versions field as a high severity finding regardless of protocol policy, since the checklist doesn't condition on it, so EEXAMPLE000024 stacks SEC-01 critical, SEC-02 critical, and SEC-04 high — a strong candidate. EEXAMPLE000043 is back to the simple single S3 OAI pattern with just the allow-all critical, but EEXAMPLE000017 is another heavy hitter — a direct EC2 origin with http-only policy (critical SEC-02) plus the allow-all critical plus weak TLS versions (high), stacking three severe findings.

I keep finding more distributions like this. Going back through the batches, most single-origin S3 OAI setups only carry the allow-all critical, but EEXAMPLE000112 has a second origin pointing to httpbin.org with an http-only policy, adding another SEC-02 critical to its stack.

E3UWB1HLS6CQRI uses MediaPackage origins with match-viewer policy and older TLS versions enabled, giving it a SEC-03 and SEC-04 high severity pair, plus a medium for lacking OAC on the media origin -- but since its viewer protocol policy already redirects to HTTPS rather than allowing all, it avoids escalating to critical.

With 11 custom error responses it passes REL-04, and since behaviors restrict methods to GET/HEAD it qualifies for the static-profile WAF severity, meaning SEC-08 lands at medium rather than high. Overall this distribution shelves out as two highs and two mediums with no criticals.

Moving to EEXAMPLE000116, I see a single S3 origin using OAI with an allow-all policy, which is already shaping up as another critical case.

For EEXAMPLE000101, two S3 OAI origins both have allow-all policies and the cache behavior does too, so I'm flagging just one critical issue there.

Then EEXAMPLE000073 stands out because its origin points directly at an EC2 instance over HTTP-only, which triggers a critical SEC-02 finding for unencrypted origin traffic.

E1TPT3FYEEMQ48 stacks two criticals: a direct HTTP-only EC2 origin (SEC-02) plus an allow-all default behavior (SEC-01), making this one of the worse distributions so far.

Continuing the sweep: GT0PITR2W has an S3 website origin flagged as a medium exception for HTTP-only, plus an allow-all critical, totaling one critical. E9P8G9K9VEHR has a single S3 OAI origin with allow-all critical but correctly configured response headers policy, and serves as the primary CDN for a staging distribution — one critical there too. EEXAMPLE000010 is already accounted for with its two stacked criticals.

Moving on, YCDCQ8O0XH and EEXAMPLE000109 both just carry the standard allow-all critical with properly configured S3 OAI origins. But EEXAMPLE000089 stands out — its origin access identity field is empty, meaning there's neither OAI nor OAC protecting it, which triggers a high-severity finding for an unrestricted S3 REST origin likely exposing a public bucket, stacking on top of the usual allow-all critical and its role as a staging distribution's primary origin — a real notable combination of issues. Now starting on the next batch with E34ZYNE961D.

NRS looks like one of the better-configured distributions: it uses a modern OAC, HTTPS-only origin, response headers policy, and a cache policy ID, so it passes most checks — but it still trips the TLSv1_2016 ACM certificate high-severity finding, giving it just one HIGH overall. EEXAMPLE000098 repeats the familiar pattern of one critical plus one high with OAC in use. Then EEXAMPLE000074 shows the same empty-OAI issue as before on its amzn-s3-demo-bucket-073 origin, stacking critical and high severities — and I notice this origin domain exactly matches the one in EEXAMPLE000089, meaning these two distributions share the same unprotected S3 bucket, with EEXAMPLE000036 potentially tied into this same pattern too.

A third distribution with a "amzn-s3-demo-bucket-039" bucket also has the same empty-OAI pattern, confirming a systemic cluster of three distributions all pointing to unrestricted "sesinbound" family buckets — something worth calling out as a related group rather than three isolated findings. EEXAMPLE000080 and EEXAMPLE000092 both proxy to httpbin.org with HTTPS-only origin policies but allow weak TLS versions, each racking up two highs (weak protocol support plus the 2016 ACM policy) while sitting disabled and orphaned. EEXAMPLE000001 stands out because its default behavior allows an unusually broad set of HTTP methods — including DELETE, PUT, and PATCH — alongside an allow-all critical finding, which is a notably risky combination.

The EEXAMPLE000001 case is more serious than it first appears: CloudFront is letting write methods like DELETE/PUT/PATCH through to an S3 website origin over plaintext, with an allow-all viewer protocol policy and no WAF, which pushes its no-WAF finding to HIGH rather than MEDIUM since it's effectively dynamic traffic. Given the critical allow-all, the website exception on origin protocol, the HIGH for missing WAF, and the unusual write-capable methods, this one deserves inclusion in the second pass despite not looking flashy on the basic checks. Several other distributions (EEXAMPLE000054, EEXAMPLE000063, EEXAMPLE000052) follow a simpler pattern — proper OAC-secured S3 origins but still flagged critical for allow-all viewer protocol, with one of them disabled and orphaned.

I'm now working through staging distributions that pair with primaries already counted (EEXAMPLE000051 pairs with EEXAMPLE000079, EEXAMPLE000001 pairs with E9P8G9K9VEHR) so I won't double-count them in the top ten, just note them as paired staging copies. For EEXAMPLE000013, which stacks critical, high, and medium findings, I'm checking whether it has a continuous deployment policy weight that affects its priority, cross-referencing the earlier CDP list to confirm the weight value for that policy ID.

I'm then reviewing EEXAMPLE000056's origin group failover setup, which only triggers on code 403 rather than the typical server error codes like 500-504, which is an unusual gap worth flagging alongside its allow-all cache behavior. Moving to EEXAMPLE000025, I'm noticing its origin domain looks like an S3 virtual-hosted-style URL but is actually configured as a custom origin with HTTP-only protocol rather than true S3 origin config, which seems like a misconfiguration worth investigating further.

This one has an origin group failover setup with good 403/404 codes but missing 5xx coverage, so it's a low-severity failover gap. Both S3 origins use OAI properly and the httpbin origin has solid TLS, but the default cache behavior still has the allow-all critical issue targeting the httpbin group.

The staging twin at EEXAMPLE000050 shares this same critical allow-all flaw but shouldn't be double-counted since it's a paired distribution. Then EEXAMPLE000037 stacks both a high-severity empty OAI issue and the allow-all critical on its amzn-s3-demo-bucket-039 origin, tying into that broader sesinbound cluster I flagged earlier, while EEXAMPLE000005 points at a lambda-url origin that's a good candidate for OAC.

That lambda-url distribution has solid HTTPS-only config but no OAC, which is a medium issue, and combined with the allow-all critical plus full write methods (DELETE/PUT/PATCH/POST) exposed means the Lambda URL is probably public and reachable directly, bypassing CloudFront entirely — though it's currently disabled, so the real-world exposure is lower for now. Then EEXAMPLE000014 stands out as one of the better-configured distributions, with WAF, OAC, response headers policy, and v2 logging all present, yet it still fails the critical allow-all check, a good illustration that even well-configured distributions share this systemic flaw.

I'm now running through the remaining distributions quickly: EEXAMPLE000096 has an S3 OAI setup but allow-all critical and is disabled; EEXAMPLE000090 and EEXAMPLE000039 are already covered, with the latter carrying two criticals (allow-all plus SSLv3 protocols); EEXAMPLE000030 passes SEC-01 cleanly with an S3 OAC origin for the Serverless Image Handler frontend; EEXAMPLE000105 has just the one high-severity TLSv1.1 issue otherwise looking solid with its API Gateway backend.

E2JKS9G8C stands out as one of the cleanest distributions overall — redirect-to-https passing SEC-01, standard logging v2 passing OPS-01, and modern TLS passing SEC-05 — worth noting as a positive example. EEXAMPLE000062 is more concerning: it has a real custom domain alias (example.org) suggesting production use, good OAC and TLS config, but logging is completely disabled, triggering an OPS-01 high finding — a strong candidate for deeper review. I'm now looking at EEXAMPLE000106, which has an "SES MCP Proxy HTTPS" comment.

This one is worse: the origin config point is HTTP-only despite a custom ALB type, triggering SEC-02 critical, plus full write methods enabled (DELETE/PUT/PATCH/POST) for what looks like a dynamic proxy, logging disabled triggering OPS-01, and no WAF — three severe findings stacked on an apparently active production workload. EEXAMPLE000032 (GameDay event UI) is comparatively minor, with just HTTP/1.1 as a low perf finding and disabled logging as the one high finding. With this depth of analysis done, I'm ready to finalize the top 10 based on severity stacking.

Ranking the final top 10 by worst severity, finding count, and production relevance: first is EEXAMPLE000091 with the most findings (two critical http-only origins, allow-all critical, no-WAF high, and two medium legacy OAI issues). Second is EEXAMPLE000106, the "SES MCP Proxy" with critical http-only ALB, no logging, and no WAF with full write methods exposed. Third is EEXAMPLE000062, which has a real custom domain alias with zero logging visibility and no WAF. I'm continuing to build out the rest of this ranked list.

Fourth is EEXAMPLE000025, which fetches an S3 bucket through a custom http-only origin bypassing all origin access control, plus allow-all. Fifth and sixth both have allow-all plus SSLv3 critical findings on MediaPackage and s3-website origins respectively. Seventh is EEXAMPLE000013 with allow-all plus a weak TLSv1-pinned ACM cert and dedicated IP cost concern. Eighth is EEXAMPLE000001 with allow-all, unusually broad write methods on an S3-website origin, and no WAF. Ninth, I'm picking EEXAMPLE000089 as the representative of the "sesinbound" cluster, with allow-all plus a high-severity S3 REST origin issue.

Rounding out the list, EEXAMPLE000017 has allow-all, a direct http-only EC2 origin, and weak origin TLS protocols. I'm now reconsidering swapping in EEXAMPLE000008, which I'd excluded despite its SSLv3 finding since it's otherwise well-hardened — SSLv3 alone is critical and worth noting. I'm also weighing EEXAMPLE000018, EEXAMPLE000024, and EEXAMPLE000072 as other strong candidates with multiple stacked critical/high findings.

Given how many distributions have 2+ critical findings, I should prioritize enabled ones for real-world risk over disabled ones, saving the latter for a rollup mention. Re-ranking the enabled candidates by severity and breadth, I'm placing EEXAMPLE000091 first, followed by EEXAMPLE000024, EEXAMPLE000017, EEXAMPLE000025, then EEXAMPLE000112, EEXAMPLE000018, and EEXAMPLE000010 as strong contenders for the remaining slots.

I still have too many "2-critical" candidates competing for a handful of top-10 spots, so I need to narrow this down further using unique signals like production domain visibility or workload identifiability.

With that I can finalize a top 10 list that balances severity, breadth, and distinctness, avoiding redundant entries that just repeat the same "custom HTTP-only origin" pattern — ranking by most findings first, then unique vulnerability combinations.

Rounding out the list: an ALB with http-only origin plus zero access logging and no WAF on what looks like a production proxy, another distribution with a real custom domain alias but the same visibility gap of no logging and no WAF, and an S3 REST origin case worth noting too.

This gives a diverse, well-justified top 10 spanning multi-origin dynamic content without WAF, http-only ALB/EC2 origins, S3 used as a public custom origin, SSLv3 exposure across a couple of distributions, zero-logging gaps, and the public-S3-bucket pattern seen in the sesinbound cluster. I'm also noting a handful of additional distribution IDs worth flagging as runners-up.

Now I want to move into Pass-2 deep dives for these top 10: pulling CloudWatch metrics for requests and 4xx/5xx errors over the past week, checking alarms, and looking at WAF associations. Checking the Wac field across all distributions, I see only one distribution outside the top 10 has a WAF ACL attached, which is worth mentioning as the sole WAF example, while all of the top 10 themselves have no WAF association at all.

I also want to check ACM certificates — only one distribution in the top 10 has a cert attached, so that's the one to run DescribeCertificate against — plus pull tags and response headers policy details where relevant for these distributions.

Setting the time window to the trailing 7 days for the metrics pull, then I'll fetch error rates and request counts, match any active alarms for CloudFront, and gather certificate and tag info for the 10 distributions in question.

I'll also need DescribeAlarms in one call and ACM DescribeCertificate once. For ListTagsForResource across the 10 distributions, I'm weighing whether that's worth the budget given these look like test resources — maybe just sample a few rather than pulling tags for all of them.

I'll skip individual tag checks for now and focus on metrics, alarms, and ACM since they're highest value. Now I need epoch timestamps for the time range.

I'm now confirming no account-wide alarms exist, no WAF ACLs to check, and the ACM cert is a watch item. With enough data gathered, I'm starting to tally summary counts across all 62 distributions, beginning with the allow-all CRITICAL findings (50 FAIL, 12 PASS) and now counting HTTP-only custom origin issues per distribution.

I'm tallying roughly 8 more distributions as HIGH severity for weak TLS versions, but recognizing that most custom origins default to allowing TLSv1 through TLSv1.2 unless explicitly restricted, so I should report these counts as approximate rather than fully precise before moving to SEC-05.

For SEC-05, I'm separating out the medium-severity default certificate cases (~53 distributions forced to TLSv1), six high-severity ACM custom domains with weak security policies, and three that pass with good policies. Then for SEC-08, I'm checking WAF coverage and finding only one distribution out of 62 actually has WAF attached.

Now I'm classifying the 61 WAF-less distributions into static versus dynamic, since dynamic origins with custom ALB/EC2/API backends warrant HIGH severity while static S3-based GET/HEAD-only distributions are MEDIUM. I'm identifying the dynamic ones with custom, ELB, and ALB origins among the no-WAF group.

Finishing the classification pass, I'm tallying that roughly 12-14 distributions qualify as dynamic (custom origins, ALB/EC2/Lambda-URL, or broad write methods) warranting SEC-08 HIGH, while the remaining ~47 with S3/media origins restricted to GET/HEAD/OPTIONS count as static and get MEDIUM.

Now I'm checking SEC-09, scanning each S3-backed distribution to see whether it's still using legacy OAI instead of the modern OAC mechanism, since most seem to be using OAI and only a handful have migrated to OAC.

Still listing distribution IDs...

Given the scope of this audit, I'll present approximate counts with clear caveats in the rollup table rather than claiming precise per-distribution verification for every single one.

For COST-01, I need to reconsider: SSLSupportMethod="vip" only triggers the dedicated-IP custom SSL charge when paired with a CUSTOM certificate (ACM/IAM), not when CloudFrontDefaultCertificate=true, since default certs don't incur that fee. Scanning the ACM-cert distributions, I found only one—E1N4W5NYGCBXAA—actually using vip method among the nine ACM-based distributions, the rest use sni.

Counting the disabled distributions, I find 9 total, and none of them use the vip+ACM combination that would escalate severity, so they all stay at LOW hygiene rather than MEDIUM.

Rolling this up, this issue affects roughly 10-12 distributions in some capacity. I think I've gathered enough depth now, so I'll start compiling the final report, though I should also verify the WAF configuration for EEXAMPLE000014 since it's the only distribution with a WAF attached, meaning I need to check wafv2.GetWebACL for it specifically.
